articleHeadline: Chandipura Vs Japanese Encephalitis: Why Similar Symptoms Need Different Diagnosis
articleSummary: Three children have died in Gujarat, India, with four more on ventilator support after a cluster of suspected Chandipura virus infections triggered a state AES alert; 32 suspected AES cases have been reported since July 1, and seven confirmed Chandipura virus patients are under 10 years old. The outbreak underscores diagnostic challenges during the monsoon when vector activity rises and AES presentations overlap. Chandipura virus (Rhabdoviridae) is spread mainly by sandflies, while Japanese encephalitis (a flavivirus) is transmitted by Culex mosquitoes; both cause fever, seizures and altered consciousness but require different public health responses. Laboratory confirmation guides control: JE is diagnosed by IgM in cerebrospinal fluid; Chandipura by RT-PCR. JE needs mosquito surveillance and evaluation of vaccination coverage; Chandipura demands intensified sandfly control, environmental measures around households and active case finding. Near-site PCR testing could shorten confirmation times and improve outbreak management.
notes: Bluedotの疾患タグは日本脳炎(Japanese Encephalitis)だが、記事の主題は実際にはグジャラート州で発生したチャンディプラウイルス感染クラスター（子供3人死亡、4人人工呼吸器管理、確定患者7人）であり、日本脳炎は鑑別診断の比較対象として言及されているのみ。実態のイベントとしてChandipura virusアウトブレイクを評価対象とした。

articleHeadline: Osaka Metropolitan University, K.K. DNAFORM, and INRB launch development of a portable rapid diagnostic system for Ebola virus disease
articleSummary: WHO declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on May 16, 2026 for Ebola virus disease caused by Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda. In response, Osaka Metropolitan University (OMU), K.K. DNAFORM, and INRB (DR Congo) launched the GenPad Smart BDBV portable rapid diagnostic system, funded by the GHIT Fund, to enable near-patient testing in resource-limited outbreak areas. A prototype developed in 40 days meets target performance: limit of detection ≤200 copies per cartridge and no cross-reactivity against 86 microbial species. The device weighs 460 g, is battery-powered (7.2 VDC, 21.6 Wh), can run eight tests per charge, and delivers results in ~30 minutes from blood collection, using fully sealed cartridges to reduce exposure. Multiple devices can be clustered for batch testing. The effort aligns with the 100-Day Mission to deliver diagnostics within 100 days of outbreak identification, leveraging OMU, DNAFORM, INRB networks and AMED support to support rapid isolation and contact tracing for BDBV, which requires tests distinct from EBOV.

Cooking likely eliminates risk, but millions in seafood farming remain at risk.

articleSummary: Zombie-ant fungi in the Ophiocordyceps unilateralis complex infect carpenter ants (Camponotus leonardi) in Thai rainforests, driving infected workers to climb vegetation and bite leaf veins about 25 cm above the forest floor. articleHeadline: High fever, body ache or chills? How to tell dengue from other monsoon fevers
articleSummary: During the monsoon, dengue, malaria and typhoid can cause fever, but each has distinct patterns. Dengue presents with sudden fever (102–103°F), severe body aches, intense headache, and retro-orbital pain; vomiting may occur and a rash can appear after 4–5 days; without timely diagnosis it can worsen. A common viral fever usually shows milder fever with cough, cold, sore throat and mild aches; vomiting and rash are less typical and recovery is quicker with rest. Malaria features high‑grade fever with chills and rigors in cyclical patterns. Typhoid develops more gradually, with fever lasting more than a week, abdominal pain and loss of appetite. No single symptom confirms dengue; diagnosis relies on symptoms, medical history, physical examination and appropriately timed laboratory tests. If dengue is suspected, avoid aspirin, ibuprofen, diclofenac and naproxen, and steroids or antibiotics are not advised for uncomplicated dengue. Seek care for warning signs such as fever >102°F, severe headache or bleeding.

articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola virus (BDBV)–related Ebola virus disease is the focus of a portable rapid diagnostic system for outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda, after the WHO declared a PHEIC on May 16–17, 2026. articleHeadline: Study reveals mechanism underlying HBV-induced liver inflammation
articleSummary: HBV-driven hepatic inflammation arises from mitochondrial dysfunction-induced ROS that activates the Nrf2-IL-6/IL-8-Jak2/Stat3 axis. In chronic HBV infection, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) genes, especially Complex I and III, are suppressed during early liver inflammation in HBV transgenic mice and human liver samples, leading to mitochondrial respiratory dysfunction and elevated ROS. Researchers from Chongqing Medical University conducted transcriptomic analyses and functional studies in HBV-replicating hepatocytes, confirming that persistent viral replication impairs respiration and increases ROS buildup, triggering Nrf2 activation and increased IL-6 and IL-8 production. These cytokines drive Jak2/Stat3 phosphorylation and transcription of inflammatory genes (Saa1, S100a9, Icam1, Socs3), promoting immune cell recruitment and hepatic inflammation. Pharmacological ROS reduction with Mito-TEMPO or HBV suppression lowers Nrf2, cytokines, Jak2/Stat3 signaling, and inflammation; NAC in pAAV/HBV1.2 mice similarly mitigates oxidative stress and pathology. The study identifies ROS-dependent Jak2/Stat3 signaling as a therapeutic target to prevent HBV-related liver disease progression.

articleSummary: Toxoplasma gondii infects about one-third of the global population, typically remaining asymptomatic and hiding in muscle and brain cells. Cats are the definitive hosts, shedding oocysts only during initial infection; most transmission worldwide arises from eating undercooked meat or exposure to contaminated soil or water. Pregnant women without prior immunity face the greatest risk, as primary maternal infection can cross the placenta and cause miscarriage, congenital blindness or neurological defects. In Australia, congenital toxoplasmosis is rare (roughly 0.17–2.3 per 10,000 births), while retinal toxoplasmosis affects about 1 in 149 Australians. Prevalence varies by region: about 50% in France and nearly 80% in Brazil. Immunocompromised individuals (e.g., post-bone marrow transplantation, HIV) risk reactivation of latent infection. Rodent studies show possible behavioral manipulation by the parasite; human links to schizophrenia are correlational, not causal. Experts urge vigilance but do not endorse panic; research seeks treatments to eradicate latent infection.
